subject: physics_2
question_text: With a neat labelled diagram explain the formation of image in a simple microscope.

mark_split.label: Magnifying power at the near point

verification.note: From FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students (physics section), Ch.2 Ray Optics and Optical Instruments, printed p.13 — Section B, 4 marks. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. The figure carries ZERO marks because the printed question does not use the phrase 'draw a neat labelled diagram of', although it does ask for a neat labelled diagram — a teacher may well award a diagram mark, and that is one of the things to confirm. Hand-checked physically: with the object inside the focal length the image is virtual, erect and magnified; for the final image at the near point D the magnifying power is m = 1 + D/f, and for the final image at infinity (object exactly at F, relaxed eye) it is m = D/f. The printed answer describes both cases in words but does not print either formula; both are added here as standard board content.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments · 4 marks

steps.label: What it is
lines: A simple microscope, or magnifier, is a
single converging lens of short focal
length.
The lens is held near the object, at a
distance of one focal length or less, and
the eye is placed close to the lens on the
other side.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two facts: one converging lens, and the object within one focal length.
steps.why: The object has to sit inside the focal length, because that is the only position where a converging lens gives an erect virtual image. Placing it outside would give a real inverted image, which the eye could not use this way.
common_mistakes: Describing two lenses. That is the compound microscope.
Placing the object outside the focal length. The image would then be real and inverted.

recall.must_convey: That a simple microscope is one converging lens of short focal length, with the object placed within one focal length.
accept: a single convex lens of short focal length
converging lens held within one focal length of the object
one lens, object inside the focal length
oke convex lens, chinna focal length
reject: m equals one plus D by f

steps.memory_tip: One lens, object inside f. Everything else follows from those five words.

steps.label: Ray diagram
steps.margin_note: The object sits inside the focal length. The two emerging rays diverge, and their backward extensions give the erect magnified virtual image.
steps.why: The dashed lines matter as much as the solid ones: they show that no light actually comes from the image, which is what the word virtual means.
common_mistakes: Drawing the image on the far side of the lens. A simple microscope forms the image on the same side as the object.

recall.must_convey: That the diagram shows the object inside the focal length, two rays through the lens, and a large erect virtual image on the same side as the object.
accept: draw the lens with the object inside the focal length
two rays diverging after the lens and extended back
the virtual image is erect and larger on the object side
reject: m equals one plus D by f

steps.memory_tip: The image is on the same side as the object, and it is drawn with dashed lines.

steps.label: Image at the near point
lines: Rays from the object are refracted by the
lens and leave it as a diverging beam.
To the eye they appear to come from a
point further away, so the image formed is
erect, virtual and magnified.
The lens is usually placed so that this
image lies at the near point, at the least
distance of distinct vision D = 25 cm, where
the eye sees it comfortably.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Three words for the image — erect, virtual, magnified — and the distance D = 25 cm.
steps.why: The image is placed at the near point because that is the closest the eye can focus, and the closer the image the larger the angle it makes at the eye. The largest useful magnification therefore comes with the image at D.
common_mistakes: Calling the image real. It is virtual, and no screen can catch it.
Writing D = 25 m or leaving D unnamed. D is the least distance of distinct vision, 25 cm.

recall.must_convey: That the image is erect, virtual and magnified, and is usually formed at the near point D = 25 cm.
accept: erect virtual and magnified image at the near point
the image is formed at twenty five centimetres
virtual image at the least distance of distinct vision
image erect virtual magnified, near point daggara
reject: m equals D by f for the relaxed eye

steps.memory_tip: Erect, virtual, magnified — the three words that describe every simple-microscope image.

steps.label: Magnifying power at D
lines: The magnifying power is the ratio of the
angle made at the eye by the image to the
angle made by the object placed at D.
With the final image at the near point,
where f is the focal length of the lens and
D = 25 cm.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Write the definition in words first, then the formula. The 1 is part of the formula.
steps.why: Magnifying power compares angles, not sizes, because what the eye judges is the angle a thing covers. A shorter focal length makes D/f larger, which is why a magnifier is a strongly curved lens.
common_mistakes: Writing m = D/f for the near-point case. That form belongs to the image at infinity.
Using f in metre with D in centimetre. Both must be in the same unit.

recall.must_convey: That the magnifying power with the image at the near point is m = 1 + D/f.
accept: m equals one plus D by f
magnifying power is one plus D over f at the near point
one plus twenty five by f
m equals one plus D by f, near point ki
reject: erect virtual and magnified image at the near point

steps.memory_tip: Near point carries the extra 1. Infinity does not.

steps.label: Image at infinity
lines: If the object is placed exactly at the focus,
at a distance f from the lens, the refracted
rays leave parallel and the image is formed
at infinity.
The eye is then fully relaxed, so this
setting is the most comfortable for long
viewing.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Object at f gives parallel rays, image at infinity, relaxed eye, and m = D/f.
steps.why: The two cases trade a little magnification for comfort: moving the object from just inside f out to f itself lowers the magnifying power by exactly 1 but lets the eye rest. That is why both formulas are worth knowing.
common_mistakes: Saying the image at infinity gives the larger magnification. It gives one less than the near-point value.
Placing the object beyond f. It must be exactly at f for the image to be at infinity.

recall.must_convey: That with the object at the focus the image forms at infinity, the eye is relaxed, and m = D/f.
accept: object at the focus gives the image at infinity and m is D by f
for the relaxed eye the magnifying power is D over f
m equals D by f when the image is at infinity
image infinity daggara ayite m equals D by f
reject: m equals one plus D by f

steps.memory_tip: Object at f, image at infinity, and the 1 disappears from the formula.

insider_note: Two settings, two formulas, and they differ by exactly 1. The near-point case is the larger one.
